body:
Thank you for your contribution. However, two problems:

- Our rules [prohibit AI for writing code beyond menial tasks](https://contributing.godotengine.org/en/latest/development/contribution_rules.html#ai-assisted-contributions). If I understand correctly, AI wrote most of the code here.
- We [do not accept new features or substantial refactors by new contributors](https://contributing.godotengine.org/en/latest/development/contribution_rules.html#no-features-from-new-contributors). Since this is a critical part of Godot core, it is not suitable for being refactored by a new contributor. 

Thank you again for your effort. If you'd like to make meaningful contributions, please consider starting with bug fixes or lower-stake refactors.

@Ivorforce Hmm, starting with a bugfix is exactly what I did in #123718, but I see your guidelines require more than 3 PRs. I think all the API adjustments, which are the bulk of this change, can be considered a menial task.

Also I didn't just dump an AI change on you. I spent weeks looking into this code and iterated on it until I couldn't improve on it further. As mentioned:

* I tried allocating each `Member` separately first.
* When I noticed it slowed down access a little (5% or so due to cache misses), I moved them back into a vector, but still shared the memory through pointers. This helped, but then of course those pointers had to be updated when the vector got reallocated.
* Then I discovered the `PagedAllocator` which solved this problem very nicely.

I guess that means the main problem is that I'm a relatively new contributor, to Godot at least. Maybe I will find some other things to fix, before resubmitting this one then.

@Ivorforce Rather than looking for other things to fix, what if I would submit this change in smaller steps? I could open a PR each for:

* Introducing the `get_member` function, which is a trivial change that just reduces the exposure to the internal data structure. I don't think it can even be considered much of a refactor on its own.

* Switching the `AHashMap`s to storing `Member*` values, pointing to instances from the `PagedAllocator`. This becomes a small but meaningful change that will significantly reduce memory usage.

It would leave out the `MemberRange` iterator for now, which is the main introduction of new code in this PR and it's not needed for most of the savings. Both changes should be easy to review.

> @Ivorforce Hmm, starting with a bugfix is exactly what I did in #123718, but I see your guidelines require more than 3 PRs.

Appreciate the thought, but yea, one change isn't enough to satisfy our rule.
But even setting the rule aside; the idea is that you get used to our processes and the code first, and then work your way up to the more complex changes.

> I think all the API adjustments, which are the bulk of this change, can be considered a menial task.

The important part of this change is the API design, not the caller fixes. That's what I'm concerned about.
New contributors are often missing the big picture, which is why we do not accept large refactors and new features from them.

> @Ivorforce Rather than looking for other things to fix, what if I would submit this change in smaller steps? I could open a PR each for:

> Introducing the get_member function, which is a trivial change that just reduces the exposure to the internal data structure. I don't think it can even be considered much of a refactor on its own.

> Switching the AHashMaps to storing Member* values, pointing to instances from the PagedAllocator. This becomes a small but meaningful change that will significantly reduce memory usage.

> It would leave out the MemberRange iterator for now, which is the main introduction of new code in this PR and it's not needed for most of the savings. Both changes should be easy to review.

Thanks for asking!
However, I'm currently not interested in the change at all (at the moment). `GDType` is still evolving, and thus it is critical for it to be simple to be adaptable to whatever changes we still need to make. Your change increases complexity.

~14mb RAM saved is very nice, but it's not a critical optimization to make at this time, I think, as it trades for more cache misses. I'm aware you benchmarked, but member access is a hot path. Your benchmark might not be representative of its true workload - the fact that your `PagedAllocator` change alleviated the 5% access burden shows that your cache held all the members accessed during your benchmark. I don't think this would be true in a game that uses lots of members across lots of classes.

Edit: Not to say I won't _ever_ be open to the change. I did definitely mean to optimize it in a similar way once the design requirements are clearer!

> The important part of this change is the API design, not the caller fixes.

I think the introduction of `get_member` does actually simplify things and definitely enables easier evolving of `GDType`, so let me know whenever you feel open for that part at least.

> Your benchmark might not be representative of its true workload - the fact that your `PagedAllocator` change alleviated the 5% access burden shows that your cache held all the members accessed during your benchmark. I don't think this would be true in a game that uses lots of members across lots of classes.

You might be right, but are you asking me to try to measure this? I think it will be hard to measure with a lot of other things going on as well, and I noticed other similar optimizations also only doing targeted benchmarking. But I could try to measure it with an actual game.

Regarding access speed, this change was already split out from a larger change which replaced the `AHashMap _members` with a plain `Vector<Member*>`, using the existing `StringName` hash as index for 10% faster member access. Since `Vector<Member*>` is smaller than `AHashMap<StringName, Member*>` and is copy-on-write, it also enables another 7.5 MB reduction of static memory (so combined with this change a 46% reduction - this is visible in the `gdtype-member-table` case in my linked benchmarks).

Anyway, I hope that eventually you will be open to these optimizations.

> > The important part of this change is the API design, not the caller fixes.
> 
> I think the introduction of `get_member` does actually simplify things and definitely enables easier evolving of `GDType`, so let me know whenever you feel open for that part at least.

I felt a little jaded by `ClassDB` re-inventing Dictionary-like functions for just about any imaginable access, often based on `List`, so I wanted to offload the interface design to an actual Dictionary type at least as long as the final needed interface is not clear yet. This still holds for me, but I realize i might be overcompensating - `get_member` isn't so bad.

> > Your benchmark might not be representative of its true workload - the fact that your `PagedAllocator` change alleviated the 5% access burden shows that your cache held all the members accessed during your benchmark. I don't think this would be true in a game that uses lots of members across lots of classes.
> 
> You might be right, but are you asking me to try to measure this? I think it will be hard to measure with a lot of other things going on as well, and I noticed other similar optimizations also only doing targeted benchmarking. But I could try to measure it with an actual game.

Only if you're interested. I'd prefer looking into other parts of the API first, and I would expect a non-benchmark scenario to be unable to escape the performance cost of the additional indirection (your `PagedAllocator` might have sent you on the wrong trail, since it made the benchmark's data easier to cache without actually fixing the problem).
To be fair, skipping `ClassDB` already made access ~50% faster, so a ~5% loss could be acceptable given the recovered memory. It's not a clearly good or bad trade.

> Regarding access speed, this change was already split out from a larger change which replaced the `AHashMap _members` with a plain `Vector<Member*>`, using the existing `StringName` hash as index for 10% faster member access. Since `Vector<Member*>` is smaller than `AHashMap<StringName, Member*>` and is copy-on-write, it also enables another 7.5 MB reduction of static memory (so combined with this change a 46% reduction - this is visible in the `gdtype-member-table` case in my linked benchmarks).

That's interesting. I'm aware on a theoretical level that iteration can be faster in scenarios of under ~100 entries, but I wouldn't expect members to be one of those use-cases. Either way, iterating `Member *` sounds like potentially tens of cache misses, which I'd expect to blow up costs under a real test. If anything, perhaps `Pair<StringName, Member*>` could work? 
But yea, that would just be my gut feeling of these conditions. I'm always happy to see numbers to a claim!

> Anyway, I hope that eventually you will be open to these optimizations.

Yes, and I really hope i haven't come across as too dismissive! 

My initial impression was worry over the combination of AI, core refactor without core background, and a hot benchmark on memory that's expected to be cold.
But i admit it's an interesting idea and i'm open to discuss it again; I'd prefer to do this after `GDType` has had more time to evolve, but if you can show address my concerns above with more tests, and re-engage to fulfill the 'new contributors' rule, we could re-open the PR too.

Feel free to come by [`#core`](https://chat.godotengine.org/channel/core) too if you're interested in talking about it more.

> Well, the trick is to start at an index in the vector based on the already available hash. Here's the core idea:
> It's an [open addressing table](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_addressing). That said, it could definitely be worth storing Pair<StringName, Member*> values in this Vector, because it would indeed make caching more effective again (but of course it uses more memory and slows down growing due to StringName reference counting).

Ah! Yes, this removes the problem, and indeed matches what I had in mind to try some time. I agree it sounds like it could be a great fit for members, even if it is adding a new hashing structure to core.
The main thing would be figuring out the details (e.g. whether to store the `name` in-vector or behind the pointer) and when to tackle this.

> The main thing would be figuring out the details (e.g. whether to store the `name` in-vector or behind the pointer) and when to tackle this.

As expected, with `Pair<StringName, Member*>` we have an even faster lookup, both cold and warm (-5% and -7.7% respectively) due to reduced deep cache and L1 misses, at the cost of somewhat slower register/unregister phases compared to storing plain `Member*` and 3.8 MB more static memory.

Then I tried `Pair<uint32_t, Member*>`, where we store just the hash part of the `StringName` in the vector. This way we avoid reference counting, speeding up register/unregister while keeping the cold read advantage.

Since due to padding the pair is as big as two pointers anyway, I also tried `Pair<const void*, Member*>`, where the pointers are `name.data_unique_pointer()`. It was the best overall according to the benchmarks. Cold reads are about 3-5% faster than current master, with fewer cache misses (the slightly higher "Cold read time (ns)" is due to CPU clock speed variation).

| VmData (MB) | 358.22 | 336.93 (-5.9%) | 340.75 (-4.9%) | 340.75 (-4.9%) |
| Instructions per read | 179.6 | 161.4 (-10.1%) | 165.0 (-8.1%) | 165.1 (-8.1%) |
| Instructions per write | 233.9 | 218.6 (-6.5%) | 221.9 (-5.2%) | 221.4 (-5.4%) |
| Cycles per warm read across classes | 100.894 | 94.755 (-6.1%) | 97.452 (-3.4%) | 95.609 (-5.2%) |
| Cold read time (ns) | 584.997 | 598.090 (+2.2%) | 548.941 (-6.2%) | 553.939 (-5.3%) |
| Cycles per cold read | 2,720.558 | 2,732.361 (+0.4%) | 2,640.507 (-2.9%) | 2,613.786 (-3.9%) |
| L1 data cache misses per cold read | 16.746 | 20.579 (+22.9%) | 19.013 (+13.5%) | 16.376 (-2.2%) |
| Cache misses per cold read | 45.487 | 49.523 (+8.9%) | 44.867 (-1.4%) | 42.112 (-7.4%) |
| Startup `[Scene] Register Types` (ms) | 25.14 | 18.60 (-26.0%) | 20.94 (-16.7%) | 20.06 (-20.2%) |
| Startup `[Core] Unregister Types` (ms) | 10.46 | 7.32 (-30.0%) | 10.14 (-3.0%) | 7.39 (-29.3%) |

</details>

But no rush with this, I just wanted to get these measurements out.
